The article is about Salt Lake City, the capital and most populous city of Utah.
Salt Lake City's population was 200,133 at the 2020 census.
Salt Lake City is the core of the Salt Lake City Metropolitan Statistical Area (MSA), which had a population of 1,257,936 at the 2020 census.
The city is further situated within a larger metropolis known as the Salt Lake City–Ogden–Provo Combined Statistical Area, comprising a population of 2,746,164 (as of 2021 estimates).
Salt Lake City has developed a strong tourist industry based primarily on skiing, outdoor recreation, and religious tourism.
The city hosted the 2002 Winter Olympics and will host the 2034 Winter Olympics.
Salt Lake City is also known for its politically liberal culture, which stands in contrast with most of the rest of the state's highly conservative leanings.
It is home to a significant LGBT community and hosts the annual Utah Pride Festival.
The city is the industrial banking center of the United States.
Salt Lake City and the surrounding area are also the location of several institutions of higher education including the state's flagship research school, the University of Utah.
Salt Lake City was founded on July 24, 1847, by early pioneer settlers led by Brigham Young who were seeking to escape persecution they had experienced while living farther east.

The Mormon pioneers, as they would come to be known, entered a semi-arid valley and immediately began planning and building an extensive irrigation network which could feed the population and foster future growth.

Salt Lake City's street grid system is based on a standard compass grid plan, with the southeast corner of Temple Square (the area containing the Salt Lake Temple in downtown Salt Lake City) serving as the origin of the Salt Lake meridian.
The city was originally named Great Salt Lake City but had "Great" dropped from its name in 1868.

Immigration of international members of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints (LDS Church), mining booms, and the construction of the first transcontinental railroad brought economic growth to the city.
The city was nicknamed "The Crossroads of the West".
It is known for its politically liberal culture, which stands in contrast with most of the rest of the state's highly conservative leanings.
Salt Lake City has a system of 85 municipal parks.
This Is the Place Heritage Park is the largest park in Salt Lake City at 217.5 acres and re-creates typical 19th century pioneer life.
Sugar House Park, known for its large, rolling hills surrounding a 4.5 acres (1.8 ha) pond with fountains, is the second largest park in Salt Lake City at 110 acres.
Red Butte Garden and Arboretum features many different exhibits and hosts musical concerts.
The city has an area of 110.4 square miles (286 km²) and an average elevation of 4,327 feet (1,319 m) above sea level.
The lowest point within the boundaries of the city is 4,210 feet (1,280 m) near the Jordan River and the Great Salt Lake, and the highest is Grandview Peak at 9,410 feet (2,868 m).
Salt Lake City has a humid continental climate with summers that are dry and hot and winters that are cold and wet.
The city's population began to stagnate during the 20th century as population growth shifted to suburban areas north and south of the city.
Few of these areas were annexed to the city, while nearby towns incorporated and expanded.
As a result, the population of the surrounding metropolitan area greatly outnumbers Salt Lake City.

The city has experienced significant demographic shifts in recent years with Hispanics now accounting for approximately 22% of residents and a large Pacific Islander population (mainly Samoans and Tongans) composing roughly 2% of the population of the Salt Lake Valley area.
Salt Lake City is subject to earthquakes from active fault lines running through it, including the Wasatch Fault which runs north–south along the western base of the Wasatch Range.
The Warm Springs Fault and East Bench Fault are offshoots of the Wasatch Fault that connect underneath Salt Lake City.
Salt Lake City has a non-partisan mayor-council form of government with the mayor and seven councillors elected to staggered four-year terms.
Many municipal elections throughout Utah are non-partisan, allowing candidates to opt for ranked choice voting.
The city's political demographics are considerably more liberal than the rest of Utah.
Since 1976, all of the city's mayors have been Democrats.

Salt Lake City is home to several non-governmental think-tanks and advocacy groups such as the conservative Sutherland Institute, the progressive Alliance for a Better Utah, the gay-rights group Equality Utah, and the quality-growth advocates Envision Utah.
The city has an eclectic music scene that includes hip hop, blues, rock and roll, rockabilly, punk, deathcore, horrorcore, and indie groups.

Popular groups or persons who started in the Wasatch Front area include Iceburn, Eagle Twin, the Almost, the Brobecks, Meg and Dia, Royal Bliss, Shedaisy, the Summer Obsession, Theater of Ice, the Used, and Chelsea Grin.

Salt Lake City is home to several museums including the Church History Museum near Temple Square, operated by the LDS Church; Clark Planetarium at The Gateway; Utah Museum of Fine Arts and Natural History Museum of Utah on the University of Utah campus; Daughters of Utah Pioneers Memorial Museum; Fort Douglas Military Museum; Social Hall Heritage Museum; and The Leonardo, a new art, science, and technology museum.

The city has a thriving festival culture with various festivals celebrating diversity in communities, including the Utah Pride Festival, Utah Arts Festival, Dark Arts Festival, Jewish Arts Festival, Sugar House neighborhood's July 4th arts festival, Sundance Film Festival, FilmQuest, Salty Horror Con & Film, Damn These Heels, and Tumbleweeds film festival for kids.
Salt Lake City is host to a number of conventions including Salt Lake Comic Con, FanX (Fan Experience), Crystal Mountain Pony Con, International Tattoo Convention, Fantasy Con, and Gaming Convention.
The city has hosted the 2002 Winter Olympics and will host the 2034 Winter Olympics.

Salt Lake City's main library system consists of the main library downtown and five branches in various neighborhoods. The main library opened in 2003 and was designed by renowned architect Moshe Safdie.
The Salt Lake City Public Library was named "Library of the Year" by the American Library Association in 2006.

Salt Lake City is home to several classic movie theaters including the Tower Theatre and Broadway Theater, both hosting the Salt Lake Film Society members and shows. The Utah Film Center hosts free film screenings every Tuesday night at the Salt Lake Public Library and monthly at the Rose Wagner Theater.

The city has a few major shopping centers such as Trolley Square, an indoor and outdoor mall with independent art boutiques, restaurants, and national retailers; Gateway, an outdoor shopping mall featuring many national restaurants, clothing retailers, a movie theater, Clark Planetarium, Discovery Gateway (formerly The Children's Museum of Utah), the Olympic Legacy Plaza, and City Creek Center.
The Salt Lake City Fire Department operates out of 14 fire stations.

Salt Lake City is near several world-class ski and summer resorts including Snowbird, Alta, Brighton, Solitude, Park City Mountain Resort, and Deer Valley. These resorts cater to millions of visitors each year and offer year-round activities.

The Salt Lake Gallery Stroll presents free evening visual art in galleries and other art-related businesses staying open late after hours. Sidewalk artists, street performers, and musicians participate in these monthly events.

Salt Lake City is home to several professional sports teams including the Utah Jazz of the NBA who play their home games at the Delta Center (formerly known as EnergySolutions Arena and later Vivint Arena); Real Salt Lake of Major League Soccer who play at Rio Tinto Stadium; and the Utah Hockey Club, which began playing in the National Hockey League's Central Division starting from 2024.

The city has a rich history with many historical buildings such as Thomas Kearns Mansion (now the Governor's Mansion), City and County Building (built 1894), the Kearns Building on Main Street, St. Mark's Episcopal Cathedral (built 1874), and the Roman Catholic Cathedral of the Madeleine (built 1909).
